subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF AMBASSADOR TO UNITED STATES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF AMBASSADOR TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce the appointment of Mr. Charles S. A. Ritchie as ambassador of Canada to the United States of America. Mr. Ritchie, who is at present permanent representatives of Canada to the United Nations, will succeed Mr. A. D. P. Heeney.
I should like to pay tribute to the outstanding service rendered by Mr. Heeney in his two tours as Canadian ambassador in Washington. He has rightly earned the highest commendation for his devoted and highly successful role as Canada's representative in the United States. His next assignment and the name of Mr. Ritchie's successor at the United Nations will be the subject of announcements at an early date.
Since joining the Department of External Affairs in 1934 Mr. Ritchie, who studied at the University of King's College, Halifax, Oxford, Harvard and the Ecole Libre de Sciences Politiques in Paris, has held a variety of important appointments at home and abroad. His first assignment abroad was in Washington in 1936 and during the war years he was a member of the high commissioner's staff at Canada house in London. He later served as counsellor at the Canadian embassy in Paris. In 1950 he became an assistant under secretary of state for external affairs, and in 1952 he was appointed deputy under secretary. He was appointed ambassador to the Federal Republic of Germany and head of the military mission, Berlin, in 1954. In 1957 he was appointed permanent representative of Canada to the United Nations. As Canada's representative there he made a valuable contribution in furthering Canadian aims in the world forum. We believe that Mr. Ritchie is particularly well qualified to discharge the important duties of head of the Canadian diplomatic mission in Washington.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF AMBASSADOR TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all hon. members of the house will have heard with great interest about the appointment
of Mr. Ritchie to this very important diplomatic post of Canadian ambassador to the United States, a post which has been filled with such great distinction, as the Prime Minister said, for some years now by Mr. Heeney, whose retirement we all regret. Mr. Heeney has not only served Canada well in Washington but in many other capacities, and I have no doubt there will be some opportunity for the country to avail itself of his services again in the future.
If Mr. Heeney is to leave Washington I can think of no better man in the Canadian diplomatic service to take his place than Mr. Charles Ritchie. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, he is an officer with great experience and ability and he has discharged, I think, all the duties that he has been asked to discharge with great efficiency and devotion. We on this side feel that this is a first class appointment, and we wish Mr. Ritchie well in his new post.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF AMBASSADOR TO UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this group heartily endorses the remarks of the leader of the official opposition with respect to the services Mr. Heeney has rendered Canada as Canadian ambassador to the United States, and with respect to the service rendered in the past to Canada by Mr. Ritchie and the greater service he now has the opportunity to render through his appointment as Canadian ambassador to the United States.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1962-63 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1963, was presented by Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) and read by Mr. Speaker to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1962-63 EXPLANATORY STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have introduced the main estimates for the new fiscal year commencing April 1, 1962. They contemplate total budgetary expenditures of $6,276.2 million. Taking account of the result of the new fiscal arrangements with the provinces, this represents a decrease of $203.4 million as compared with a total of $6,479.6 million provided in the estimates tabled to date for the present fiscal year. Further details are available in a
752	HOUSE OF
Tabling of Main Estimates statement which has been issued to the press in keeping with the practice and on the terms prevailing for many years.
I should like to draw to the attention of the house certain notable changes which hon. members will find in the form and content of the estimates. During the session of 1960-61 the standing committee on public accounts of the House of Commons examined the form and content of the estimates. The committee in its report to the House of Commons on June 20, 1961 recommended several changes in the form of the estimates. All of these changes have been implemented in the main estimates for 1962-63.
The changes are of two types; first, those related to the form of the estimates, such as:
(a)	the introduction of a new "permanent numbers" vote numbering system;
(b)	the inclusion of vote numbers in the details section;
(c)	the addition of a table of contents to the estimates book;
(d)	the rearrangement of the sequence of information so that the details section of each departmental class would be located immediately following the vote section for that class.
The second type of change concerns the content of the estimates. Here the committee recommended the distribution, for information purposes, of the costs of major common services which are provided to other departments without a corresponding charge to their appropriations. It also recommended the rearrangement of staff detail in a manner which would result in a clearer understanding of establishment proposals.
An improved vote numbering system has been devised which will allow the printing of vote numbers in the details of estimates without causing delays in tabling estimates. It also has other advantages over the numbering system used heretofore. The essence of the new system is that annually recurring votes will be designated by the same vote numbers from year to year and supplementary votes will bear the same basic numbers as their related main estimates votes.
A criticism of Canadian estimates in the past has been that the total cost of a particular departmental area was difficult to assess because the estimates for that department did not contain provision for common services which were performed by other government agencies and provided to them free of charge. To assist in arriving at a reasonable picture of total cost without the introduction of costly accounting practices, there is now included in the details of services for each area identified in the over-all summary in the front of the blue book a list of the major services


provided free of charge to that department together with their estimated costs. In addition, the cost of accommodation provided in earlier estimates is now shown.
Salary details accounted for about 200 of the 610 pages in the blue book for 1961-62 and involved departments in thousands of man hours of work calculating their detailed costings. Moreover, because of its size and complexity its value to members of parliament as supporting detail for the "Salaries" object of expenditure was considered questionable. A new form of staff detail has been adopted in which the total personnel establishment provided for in each vote is first divided, to show tenure or security of employment, into "Continuing Establishment" and "Casuals and Others". For the former, both numbers of positions and their man year equivalents are provided. The addition of man years for "Casuals and Others" provides a measure in other than dollar terms for the total establishment.
The committee in its report invited attention to other possible changes. These are under study and will be discussed in due course with the standing committee on public accounts. It is considered that the changes recommended by the committee and incorporated in these estimates represent a major improvement.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture, who as hon. members know is ill, I wish to announce that the agricultural stabilization board will make a deficiency payment of 22 cents a pound on the 1961 wool clip. This payment compares with the deficiency payment of 23 cents a pound paid on the 1960 wool clip last year.
The deficiency payment is calculated as the difference between the stabilization price of 60 cents a pound and the average market price per pound f.o.b. Toronto for the basic grades western range choice, half blood staple, and eastern domestic, quarter blood staple, combined.
It is estimated that the 1961 production of wool will be the same as the 1960 wool clip of approximately 6 million pounds.
Cheques to producers for deliveries of 20 pounds or more of eligible graded wool which have been reported to the agricultural stabilization board will be issued as soon as possible, and it is expected they will be mailed within the next three or four weeks.

speechtext:
1.	Since January 1, 1961, have the governments of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario made any agreements with the federal Department of Labour concerning the assistance granted by the said department under the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act?
2.	If so, what amounts will the province of Quebec receive pursuant to the said agreements?
3.	What amounts will the province of Ontario receive pursuant to the same agreements?

Questions
Answer by: Mr. Starr:
1.	Yes.
2.	Pursuant to the technical and vocational training agreement, the federal government pays to the province of Quebec the following percentage of contributions to provincial expenditures incurred on the programs listed:
Vocational high school program: Up to an annual allotment of $877,300. The estimated annual payment for 1961-62 is $500,000.
Technician training program: 50 per cent of provincial costs. The federal payment for the fiscal year 1961-62 is estimated to be $4,950,000.
Trade and other occupational training program: 50 per cent of provincial costs. For the fiscal year 1961-62 the federal payment is estimated at $3,000,000.
Training in co-operation with industry: 50 per cent of provincial costs. For the fiscal year 1961-62 the federal payment is estimated at $60,000.
Student aid: Annual allotment of $100,000, or 50 per cent of provincial expenditures, whichever is the lesser.
Training of disabled persons: 50 per cent of provincial costs. For the fiscal year 1961-62 the federal payment is estimated at $200,000.
Training of technical and vocational teachers: 50 per cent of provincial costs. For the fiscal year 1961-62 the federal payment is estimated at $65,000.
Technical and vocational correspondence courses: 50 per cent of provincial costs. For the fiscal year 1961-62 the federal payment is estimated at $62,500.
Training of unemployed persons: 75 per cent of provincial costs for each fiscal year if the number of student training days in that fiscal year exceeds 226,400. If this minimum number of student days is not exceeded in any fiscal year the federal contribution will be 50 per cent of provincial costs. Estimated federal payments for the fiscal year 1961-62 are $1,125,000.
The total estimated federal payments for the fiscal year 1961-62 for these operational programs will be in the neighbourhood of $10,000,000 for the province of Quebec.
In addition, the federal government contributes 75 per cent of approved capital expenditures (buildings and equipment) incurred prior to April 1, 1963 and 50 per cent thereafter to March 31, 1967 used for technical and vocational training. The contribution to provincial expenditures under this category for the fiscal year 1961-62 in the province of Quebec is estimated at $3,800,000.
3.	The technical and vocational training agreement with the province of Ontario is identical to that entered into with the province of Quebec with the exception that the
(Mr. Bourbonnais.l
annual allotment for vocational high school training in Ontario is limited to a federal payment of $823,800. The ultimate federal contribution to the province of Ontario for all programs under the agreement for the fiscal year 1961-62 is estimated at $44,000,000. The larger federal payment to Ontario as compared to Quebec for the fiscal year 1961-62 is due principally to a more extensive capital building program being carried on by Ontario during the current fiscal year than is the case in the province of Quebec, i.e. in the province of Quebec, the federal government has approved, to date, of ten capital projects submissions by the province, involving a total federal payment of approximately $5,000,000, whereas in the province of Ontario, 143 projects submissions have been approved, involving an estimated federal payment of approximately $119,000,000.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: DISARMAMENT
subsubtopic: INVITATION TO ATTEND MEETING OF COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he has received an invitation from the head of the Soviet government to attend, as head of the Canadian government, the forthcoming meeting on March 14 I believe, of the United Nations disarmament commission and, if so, has he any observation to make on that invitation?
Bight Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, if the house will permit me I will answer this question in some detail. I have received a message from Chairman Khrushchev which was handed me directly by the Soviet ambassador. As is now generally known, Mr. Khrushchev addressed a note to all members of the 18-nation disarmament committee proposing that the heads of government should be present when the disarmament conference begins its work in Geneva on March 14. This note was in the nature of a reply to the joint message of February 7 from Prime Minister Macmillan and President Kennedy respecting which I made a statement on Thursday last.
I am not yet in a position to indicate what the Canadian government's response will be to Mr. Khrushchev's counter proposal.
The letter was a lengthy one which will have to be studied as a whole so that the full implications of his specific proposal may be assessed. It will also be necessary to consult with other interested governments to determine what procedure will best contribute to progress on disarmament. The Canadian government has taken the stand that the forthcoming disarmament negotiations should be made the occasion of a maximum, all-out effort toward disarmament.
The hon. member for Kootenay West gave me notice of a similar question and in particular respecting the latter part of the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition. If that purpose, namely the attainment of an all-out effort toward disarmament, would be served by meetings at the heads of government level, I am sure the house would expect me to be prepared to attend.

speechtext: May I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Has the minister any comment to make on press reports to the effect that a Canadian judge has been appointed president of the high court in Cyprus?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF CANADIAN AS PRESIDENT OF HIGH COURT
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF CANADIAN AS PRESIDENT OF HIGH COURT
speechtext: May I say the question goes beyond the orders of the day, but if the minister wishes to comment on it I do not see any reason why he should not.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF CANADIAN AS PRESIDENT OF HIGH COURT
speechtext:
Some months ago the government of Cyprus requested Canadian co-operation in filling this important judicial post. The high court of Cyprus is the highest appellate

court of the republic. It is composed of two Greek judges, one Turkish judge and a president with two votes. The Cypriot constitution specifies that the court cannot function without a president and that the presiding judge cannot be a subject or a citizen of the republic of Cyprus, the kingdom of Greece, the republic of Turkey, or of Britain or its colonies. The first president of the high court was His Honour Judge Barra O'Briain of Ireland, whose term was for a one year period only.
Before Judge O'Briain ended his term, the government of Cyprus asked the Canadian government for assistance in selecting a Canadian jurist, and negotiations concerning this post have been proceeding for some months both in Canada and through our mission to Cyprus. The Cypriot authorities have now appointed a distinguished Canadian jurist, Mr. Justice J. L. Wilson of the Ontario supreme court.
I think hon. members will agree that the appointment of Mr. Justice Wilson reflects great credit on Canada and indicates the degree of respect which Canadian justice and Canadian jurists enjoy overseas.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the government is glad that this new member of the commonwealth requested assistance from us as an older member of the commonwealth. We think the selection by the Cypriot government of a Canadian judge for this position provides another close link in the friendly relationship which exists between our two commonwealth countries.

speakeroldname: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM WHITECOURT, ALBERTA
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize and to provide for the construction of a line of railway in the province of Alberta by Canadian National Railway Company from White-court for a distance of approximately 23.2 miles to the property of Pan American Petroleum Corporation, at a total estimated expenditure of $2,300,000, not to be exceeded by more than fifteen per cent; to authorize the issue by the said railway company of securities that may be guaranteed by Her Majesty in right of Canada to finance the construction of the said line; and in order that the said railway company may forthwith proceed with the construction of the said line of railway, to authorize temporary loans to the said railway company out of the consolidated revenue fund upon terms and conditions prescribed by the governor in council and secured by securities of the said railway company.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Martineau in the chair.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM WHITECOURT, ALBERTA
speechtext:
The proposed legislation would authorize the Canadian National Railway Company to construct a railway line in the province of Alberta as an extension of its Sangudo subdivision, from Whitecourt, Alberta, in a westerly direction to the property of Pan American Petroleum Corporation in the Windfall gas field area, a distance of about 23 miles.
The main function of this line would be the transportation of sulphur which will be produced from natural gas on the property of Pan American Petroleum Corporation in the Windfall area.
The cost of construction of the line is estimated at a total of $2,300,000 or an average of $99,138 per mile, including the cost of a steel bridge about 650 feet long across the McLeod river at the eastern end of the line.
A sulphur recovery plant is now under construction in the Windfall area. Plans call for initial shipments of sulphur to be made from the plant by March 1, 1963. Texas Gulf

Sulphur, the operator of the plant, has notified the railway that direct rail service will be needed by that date.
The construction of this line will take about one year, and in order that the railway may complete the line by March 1, 1963, it is essential that some of the work on the piers and abutments of the bridge over the McLeod river near Whitecourt be done during the period of low water in the present winter season. This means that a start must be made on this work immediately. The committee will therefore, I am sure, appreciate the importance of giving consideration to this legislation will contain financial provisions measure can be adopted by an early date, work will thereby be provided this winter for a substantial number of men, thus contributing in a not insignificant way to the provision of employment in this locality.
The legislation would empower the spending of a sum not exceeding $2,645,000, representing the total estimated cost of construction of $2,300,000 plus 15 per cent for contingencies, to build this rail line. The legislation will contain financial provisions similar to those adopted in the past for other railway branch lines.
Canadian National has informed the government that an agreement has been signed with Texas Gulf Sulphur Company wherein a guarantee is given that they will ship a minimum volume of traffic over the line for 25 years, and that appropriate penalties will be paid by them to the railway if at any period during that term the guaranteed shipments fall below the minimum volume agreed to. In addition they have agreed to make a substantial cash contribution toward the cost of construction of the line.
As members are aware, the government views with favour and is desirous of giving continued encouragement to capital projects submitted by the railway management which can be recognized as self-liquidating. The present project is in that category. Railway revenues which will be received from traffic generated by the line after meeting all expense of operation and maintenance of the branch line, including the cost of handling this traffic on the remainder of the system, interest on and amortization of the cost to the railway of building the new line, will yield a reasonable surplus.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM WHITECOURT, ALBERTA
speechtext:
I have listened with interest to the remarks made by the minister in connection with this resolution which seeks, on behalf of the C.N.R., authority to build a line from Whitecourt in the province of Alberta to the property of the Pan American Petroleum Corporation, a distance of 23.2 miles.
Canadian National Railways
The minister has told the committee something about the economics of the line. At first blush, without knowing all the details concerning the operation, it would seem to us on this side that the project is a meritorious one which will receive our approval. If I understand the matter correctly, the resolution will authorize the Canadian National Railway Company to build a line in a westerly direction to a sour gas well on the property of the Pan American Petroleum Corporation, and it is the intention of the petroleum corporation to convert this sour gas to sulphur, an operation which would mean the exportation of that commodity over the C.N.R. system not only to the United States but to parts of Canada.
The cost, the minister has said, will be $2,300,000 or an average of $99,138 per mile including the cost of building a steel bridge. The minister did say in the course of his remarks that a substantial contribution toward the construction of this line would be made by, I take it, the Pan American Petroleum Corporation. The minister did not say what the amount of that contribution would be, but I take it the amount whatever it is, will reduce the expenditure of $2,300,000 accordingly. So if a contribution of, say $1,800,000 were made by the petroleum corporation, then the C.N.R. would be asked to disburse toward the construction of this line the difference between the two sums, namely $500,000. I trust that when the minister replies he will be in a position to confirm or contradict the information I have placed on record in this respect.
The minister also stated that a sulphur recovery plant is now under construction and will be completed, according to expectations, by March 1, 1963. That is why, he said, it is important that the bridge over the McLeod river, a bridge which will be some 600 to 650 feet in length, be constructed without delay. I am informed that the bridge which is near, if not very close, to the beginning of the line will require four spans with three centre piers in the river, and that these piers must be put down in the winter time. I am also informed that the construction of these piers is a simple matter when ice conditions exist, but that the moment the thaw begins this would be a complicated matter from a construction standpoint.
I wish the minister would clarify the statement he has made in this respect because if this is so, if there is likely to be a delay of 12 months should the piers not be put down under winter conditions, then I am sure these circumstances would have a bearing on the attitude which those of us on this side of the chamber would wish to take toward the government's proposal. In

Canadian National Railways other words, I am sure none ol us would wish to delay what appears to be a very profitable enterprise on the part of the Canadian National Railways if it is necessary that these piers must be put down under winter conditions.
It was also stated by the minister that it would take one year to build this line. When the minister replies will he indicate why it will take a year, in view of the fact that we are asked to give immediate approval to this legislation. I wish the minister would also tell us how the cost per mile compares with that of other lines in the area. When I say "in the area" I do not necessarily mean in the province of Alberta, because I do not recollect that other lines have been built there recently, but certainly other lines have been built in adjoining provinces. Perhaps the minister could give some indication of how the cost of this line compares with that of others.
I feel the minister should give the committee some further details concerning the agreement which has been made between the Canadian National Railways and, I presume, the Pan American Petroleum Corporation in so far as traffic is concerned. It has been the practice of the minister, more particularly in relation to the railway to Great Slave lake which was discussed during the last session of parliament, to table the agreement so the committee could have before it for consideration and study all the details of the financial arrangements. We are interested in examining the profitable aspect of this line which will improve the position of the Canadian National Railways.
The minister also gave us a general idea of the revenues which it will yield to the railway over a period of time. I understand the agreement is for a period of 25 years, and I am sure like most comparable agreements it is lengthy and complicated. Perhaps the minister or his officers would assist the committee by summarizing the main points of the agreement. After all, there is never any difficulty about obtaining approval for the construction of lines like this, particularly when the financial conditions are similar to those the minister indicated earlier. It has not been my experience that parliament withholds its approval in these circumstances. If the minister would be good enough to summarize for us or, in the alternative, table the agreement, I feel it would be helpful and would assist those on this side of the house who would like to give it further consideration.
I take it, too, that when the appropriate time arrives the minister will wish to move that this legislation be referred for consideration to the committee on railways, canals


and telegraph lines. I hope the minister will find it possible to follow that course later this day.
Having regard to what I have said and in the light of the questions I have asked, there will be from this side of the house no objection to the construction of this project which on the face of it appears to be a profitable enterprise for the Canadian National Railways.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM WHITECOURT, ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased that this legislation has come before the house so early in the session. As the minister has said, it is a matter of immediate urgency to provide for the construction of the bridge across the McLeod river on the outskirts of the town of Whitecourt in the northwestern portion of my constituency. This project is one of the major developmental projects which fits into a vast complex of development which is taking place in northwestern Alberta.
I wish to tell hon. members of the committee something of the Windfall field and something of the potential of the Whitecourt area, and to make the prediction that the next city in Alberta will be called Whitecourt. For the information of the hon. member for Laurier I will say the plant is practically ready to go into production. A substantial acreage has been cleared for the purposes of storing sulphur until such time as the railway line is built, and it is most important that the line be constructed as soon as possible.
The Windfall field is a sour gas field located 23 miles west of Whitecourt. The extraction plant at Windfall serves a combination of three fields through a very intricate and complicated system of pipe lines. The gas has a high sulphur content. The high pressure gas from the Pine Creek and Beaver Creek fields north of Edson passes into the Windfall field. The Windfall gas field is a wet gas area. The two high pressure gas fields are being used to supply the pressure and the Windfall field is supplying the reservoir.
The plant when completed will be producing approximately 650 tons of sulphur a day, a fair quantity. This will mean an annual output of approximately 237,000 long tons of sulphur. It is expected that within five years the plant will triple its output and will produce in the neighbourhood of 614,000 long tons of sulphur per year.
I am sure the committee will be interested if I take a moment to discuss the sulphur situation in Canada. Up until 1952 all elemental sulphur was imported, mostly from the United States and Mexico, but in the last few years Canada has become an important sulphur producing nation. Approximately 30 per cent of Canadian produced sulphur is

Canadian National Railways
being produced from natural gas, and this will rise to approximately 75 per cent. Approximately 75 per cent of the sulphur produced in Canada will come from the gas fields of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. The total annual capacity of elemental sulphur will reach approximately 1,500,000 tons annually from these western gas fields.
During 1960 the total amount of sulphur used in Canada was 600,000 tons. As hon. members will see, this one plant in the Windfall area will, within the next two or three years, be producing sufficient sulphur to meet Canada's present needs. Sulphur being one of the basic minerals used in industry, we expect the demand for it will increase.
The Windfall plant is only one of approximately 14 plants in Alberta that are extracting sulphur from natural gas. This is fundamentally a by-product operation through which wet and sour natural gas is made available for export in a dry and clean form. The gas from the Windfall field, after it is treated and the sulphur and the other wet hydrocarbons are extracted from it, is going directly into the Alberta Southern pipe line and will eventually end up in California. It is in this immediate area that we had that tragic accident about a month ago when a section of pipe line blew up. I am sure this accident illustrates the dangers that still remain and the hardships which are ahead of those who are now pioneering in an unsurveyed part of Canada.
As I have already said, we are pleased that the government has brought this legislation forward quickly so that we can go ahead with the construction of this railway. I should like to say that we feel that railway will be the first 23 miles in a western Alberta net of railways which will be constructed in the next five years and which will consist of some 150 miles of railway through new country of which, so far as its potential is concerned, the surface has only been scratched. I suggest to the committee that we shall here in the area adjacent to Whitecourt set the stage for a sulphur production plant and for other mineral developments which will necessitate much more railway building. We hope that eventually we shall have a smelter in the immediate area.
As I have said, this railway extends from the town of Whitecourt, which at the moment is at the stage of bustling and booming because of the extraction plant, the coming of the railway and our hope that a new newsprint plant will be built next spring. I am confident that this railway will haul not only sulphur but pulpwood as well, will open up new areas for logging, will be an asset to the Canadian National Railways and will 26207-1-
at all times provide an appropriate return. I am convinced that the necessary tonnage is available in order to satisfy the guarantee. I am convinced that at no time will the taxpayers be called upon to subsidize this railway line or to support it in any other manner. This is a project which fits in now with our government's development policy, and in the future will fit in with other railway construction in Canada. I am pleased that the official opposition are not going to do to this railway what they did to the Great Slave lake railway we are going to build in Alberta, namely vote against it.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM WHITECOURT, ALBERTA
speechtext:
I was just waiting for the cordial invitation, Mr. Chairman. First of all may I say that I am pleased to hear from the hon. member for Laurier that the opposition does not intend to delay the proceedings but will support this resolution so that we can go ahead with the building of this line as soon as possible. I also wish to commend my friend the hon. member for Jasper-Edson for his comprehensive survey of the sulphur situation in Canada and in general for his description of the various natural resources which are so abundant in that great riding of his.
It is true that this branch line project is another example of the tremendous wealth of natural resources we find in this great province of Alberta. When we think of the relatively recent discoveries that have been made in that province we are indeed fascinated to contemplate the great future that lies ahead for Alberta. I am sure that as Canadians all members of the committee will rejoice in seeing these great developments.
To come back to the hon. member for Laurier, may I say this. Again he indicates that he would like the minister to table the agreement between the railway company and the private company. I would just refer him back to our discussion of last year and the discussions that took place under former ministers of transport on previous branch line bills. I should also refer him to his own statements before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I do so in order that he will understand why I am not in a position at the present time to disclose the various aspects of the agreement. I wish to repeat what I said earlier, namely that this

Canadian National Railways is a branch line that represents a very great deal for the Canadian National Railways. A private company has agreed to contribute substantially to the construction of the branch line. It has also agreed-and I think this is a most important factor-to give an undertaking or a guarantee of a minimum tonnage of sulphur and other goods to be transported on the branch line. It has also agreed to pay a penalty for any amount of tonnage below that set level.
I know it would be much more interesting to the hon. member for Laurier if I could simply give all the details of the agreement. However, I think the request of the railway should be complied with. We must not forget that the Canadian National Railway is obliged to compete with other railways in Canada. As it is a government owned railway, if we disclose here in the House of Commons all the private agreements the railway signs in a business way with private industries, I think we shall simply be putting our national railway in an unfair position compared with its main competitor, the Canadian Pacific Railway. I therefore ask the indulgence of the committee in this matter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM WHITECOURT, ALBERTA
speechtext: As far as the last two questions are concerned, may I say this. The information requested is precisely that which would jeopardize the position of the Canadian National Railways as a competitor with other railways in Canada. That is what would happen if we give the amount which the private company has agreed to pay for the construction of the branch line. This is the crux of the problem. This is the main point of this agreement.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM WHITECOURT, ALBERTA
speechtext: Where is the competition? This line is being constructed from a Canadian National Railways line so where is the competition with any other line?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM WHITECOURT, ALBERTA
speechtext:
In this precise case, of course, this line is to be built by Canadian National Railways, but on the other hand I think that the business world and private companies of this type like to keep their own financial agreements with respect to transportation costs and other costs to themselves. They do not like to have to divulge that information to their competitors. I am speaking now of private companies like the sulphur company. They are not interested in giving all these figures to their competitors with whom they have to fight for business. I am sure the hon. member for Laurier understands this.
Of course, as far as the government is concerned, we would be quite willing to do that if it would not jeopardize the position of Canadian National Railways, and that is why we agreed to do it last year when the Pine Point railway measure was before the house. As you know, Mr. Chairman, that was a development project in which the government was subsidizing the construction of the railway and it also involved an agreement between the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, which is a subsidiary of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the government, and Canadian National Railways. The fact that the mine was a subsidiary of the main competitor of Canadian National Railways more or less removed the difficulty. In this case the project is one that will pay for itself and will result in a surplus to Canadian National Railways. It is a good business deal for the railway, and I think it would be very unfortunate if we were to do anything to spoil this splendid project. The private sulphur company is satisfied to pay the price it is going to pay and the management of Canadian National Railways have assured the government that with this agreement they will be in a very good position to build this branch line and operate it without it costing Canadian taxpayers a cent.
The hon. member for Laurier asked why the piers have to be built at this precise time and why there should be as much diligence as possible in having the legislation passed by parliament. I am informed by the engineers of Canadian National Railways that quite a large bridge has to be built over the McLeod river. As hon. members know, with a river of this type there is a tremendous difference in the depth of the water in the spring and summer compared with the middle of winter. Right at this precise time the water level is perfect for the building of this type of bridge because the water is very low during this coldest

time of the year and the construction people will practically be in a position to build these two piers on dry land.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM WHITECOURT, ALBERTA
speechtext: Are there two or three?

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM WHITECOURT, ALBERTA
speechtext:
Either two or three. I have not studied the exact engineering of this particular bridge. I am assured by the engineers that the period of maximum use as far as soil is concerned with respect to the building of these piers is right now, and that period will not last very long. They have impressed upon me the urgency of going ahead with this project as soon as possible.
The sulphur company has already started to build its plant at the future terminal of the railway and it has requested the C.N.R. to complete the railway by next March. The engineers of the railway assure me that if the bridge can be started within a very few days they will be in a very good position to meet this deadline. This is extremely important because, as I said earlier, this is an excellent deal for the government owned railway, and it would be most unfortunate indeed if we were to delay the actual starting of construction of the bridge and in this way spoil the whole agreement. I think I have covered the points raised by the hon. member for Laurier and again I want to congratulate the hon. member for Jasper-Edson for his very fine contribution to this debate.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION AND PURCHASE OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is to authorize Canadian National Railway Company to construct an eight mile extension to its recently completed railway line between Optic lake and Chisel lake in the province of Manitoba, at a cost estimated at $1,090,000. The extension would run from Chisel lake to Stall lake.
Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company Limited is presently mining zinc and copper in the Chisel lake area and shipping the ore to their metallurgical plant at Flin Flon, Manitoba. This company is now developing its properties in the area of Stall lake and at Osborne lake and has requested rail service to Stall lake to serve those new ore bodies by May 1, 1963. The ore from this new development will also be shipped to the company's plant at Flin Flon.
As in the case of the construction of the original branch line from Optic lake to Chisel lake, Canadian National has secured a guarantee that the mining company will ship a minimum volume of traffic over the line for a period of at least ten years and that appropriate penalties will be paid if during any year of the term the shipments fall below the minimum agreed to.
If this measure can be adopted by an early date work will be provided in the area during the present winter for a considerable number of people, thus contributing to the provision of employment in this locality. In addition to providing service for the new mines opening up in the area this extension will also aid in the further general development of this area of Manitoba.
Hon. members will note that the bill will amend chapter 13 of the Statutes of Canada, 1957-58, under which the original 52 mile line from Optic lake to Chisel lake was constructed. While that act estimated the expenditure for the 52 miles of construction at $8,840,000 the actual total cost of construction of the line, which is now in operation, has amounted to approximately $6.4 million. Since the cost of the existing branch line, plus the estimated cost of the proposed extension of eight miles only totals $7,490,000, there is no need for approval of any additional expenditure, as it is obvious that the extension can be constructed well within the amount authorized by the enabling legislation. This bill, therefore, will simply amend the schedule to the original act to show the length of the branch

Canadian National Railways line as 60 miles instead of 52 miles, leaving the estimated cost of construction unchanged at $8,840,000.
This being a capital project submitted by the railway management, which is clearly self-liquidating, the government is pleased to give its support to the measure.
Railway revenues which will be received from traffic generated by the new mines, after meeting all expenses of operation and maintenance of the extension, the cost of handling this traffic on the remainder of the system, interest on the cost of building the new line and interest and depreciation on the necessary equipment, will yield a reasonable surplus.
Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company Limited has established significant reserves of copper ore at Stall lake and also on its property at Osborne lake, some 11 miles to the northeast of Stall lake.
Capital expenditures made by the company to the end of 1961 on these properties have been substantial and it is planned to bring the Stall lake mine into production by May 1,
1963.	The mining company has therefore requested that Canadian National complete the construction of a branch line extension to its Stall lake mine as soon as possible but not later than May 1, 1963. Under a normal schedule of construction the extension would take about one year to build and the average number of men employed would be about 75.
As the Osborne lake property is developed the ore will be trucked from that mine to Stall lake and thence, together with the Stall lake ore, shipped by rail a distance of 107 miles to the company's metallurgical plant at Flin Flon. The company estimates that 100 men will be employed at Stall lake and about 85 men at Osborne lake when these mines are in production.
The prospective traffic on the proposed branch line extension will be in addition to that now being produced at the company's Chisel lake property, and will consist of copper-zinc crude ore amounting to about 182,000 tons per year.
The mining company and the railway have reached agreement on the arrangements for handling this traffic, under which the mining company has given a guarantee that it will ship a minimum volume of traffic over the line for at least 10 years and that appropriate penalties will be paid if, in any year during the term, shipments should fall below the minimum volume agreed to.
The government is convinced that this project merits the approval of the house as it is one which should improve the net position of Canadian National as well as contribute to the further development of the area concerned. The railway has given assurance that

the estimated results of operation make the proposal an attractive and economic one.
The bill will amend chapter 13 of the Statutes of Canada, 1957-58, under which the 52 mile Optic lake-Chisel lake line was built, by the substitution of a new schedule to that act calling for 60 miles of construction in place of the 52 shown.
As I said earlier, the railway's experience in constructing the 52 miles provided for in this legislation indicates that the final cost of construction of the whole 60 miles will not exceed the amount approved in the original schedule of $8,840,000, because the final cost of construction of the 52 mile line to Chisel lake has only amounted to $6,400,000, which when taken with the estimated cost of the eight mile extension of $1,090,000, gives a total for the whole 60 miles still substantially less than the amount originally approved.
On second reading being given, I intend to move that the bill be referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, where officers of the Canadian National will be present to give any further explanations.
I believe the house will agree that the project commends itself as one which will assist in the further development of this mining area, and that it is a sound one from an economic standpoint.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MANITOBA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CONSTRUCTION AND PURCHASE OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext:
There will not be the slightest hesitation on the part of the opposition to support this bill. The reasons for that will appear obvious to the house. In the first place, it was the former administration which some years ago brought before the house a proposal for the construction of a railway line from Sherridon to Flin Flon in the province of Manitoba, and it is a development of that railway which is now under consideration.
Later on, in December 1957, to be exact, the present government brought forward for consideration to the house construction by the Canadian National Railways of the line from Optic lake to Chisel lake in the province of Manitoba, being approximately 52 miles, of which we approved at that time. It was my colleague, the former minister of transport, the Hon. Mr. Marler who, speaking on that occasion, as recorded at pages 1778-79 of Hansard, December 3, 1957, had this to say:
I should like to mention to the committee that as favourable consideration was given to both of these projects by the former government of which I was a member I may assure the committee that it is not our intention to delay the passing of the resolution or the measure which will follow the adoption of the resolution. X think, however, that the presentation of this resolution does afford an appropriate occasion to emphasize the importance of railroad development to the economy of Canada.

So, the first line which I referred to, namely that from Sherridon to Flin Flon, was submitted to the house by the former Liberal administration. The next, which this one seeks to extend, was submitted to the house by the present government although it had received the approval of the former administration. The minister will remember that it was his predecessor in office who brought the original measure before the house in December of 1957, several months after the change of government. As the minister said, this bill is an amendment to chapter 13 of 6 Elizabeth II, 1957-58 Statutes of Canada, wherein the governor in council was authorized to provide for the construction by Canadian National Railway Company of the line as set out in this statute, namely a line of railway from a point on the Lynn lake railway line at or near Optic lake extending in an easterly direction to a point at or near Chisel lake, both in the province of Manitoba, a distance of 52 miles, at an average cost of $170,000 per mile and a total construction cost of $8,840,000.
I was pleased to hear the minister say that the Canadian National Railway Company has gone substantially beneath that cost, in that the total cost thus far for completion of the line is $6,400,000. If I understood the minister aright-and he will correct me if I am wrong -it was not necessary for the government to come before parliament on this occasion; they could have proceeded to build the line under the jurisdiction contained in chapter 13 of the original act to which I have just referred. If that is the case, I can of course see the reason why the government comes before parliament now. It adds the other eight miles of the line, and instead of being one of 52 miles it now becomes one of 60 miles. That being the case, this is simply an amendment to the original act of parliament of which we on this side of the house approved, in that the legislation now before the house authorizes the construction of a line from Optic lake to Chisel lake, a distance of approximately 8.2 miles. The minister has given the reasons, which are because of additional industrial mineral development in the area, to which I think all members on this side of the house would subscribe.
There are, of course, the usual questions which come to my mind again and I would ask the minister to deal with them when he replies. The first question I put to him is this: why was not a resolution required in the case of this railway, as was required in the case of the previous railway, the discussion of which we have just completed? With regard to the railway having to do with the construction from Whitecourt to the Pan American Petroleum Corporation property there is a
Canadian National Railways resolution on the order paper. With reference to the railway in the province of Quebec there is a resolution on the order paper. In respect of this bill, which will mean an expenditure, as the minister put it, of some $1,800,000, the question which first comes to my mind is, why was there not a resolution?
Then the question I raise again has to do with the guarantee. Will the minister table the guarantee, as he did on a former occasion; and if not, will he summarize for us the general terms of that guarantee? He did make some reference to it but I do not think the references are sufficient to allow us to deal with the matter as constructively as we should like, without further details.
Then the minister said that on the appropriate occasion he would refer consideration of this line to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. He did not make that statement with reference to the previous railway, and again I am prompted to ask him whether he will refer the Whitecourt-Pan American Petroleum Corporation line to the railway committee for consideration, as he intends to do in this case. I think we should have replies to those two questions. However, mainly on the ground that this is simply an amendment to an act of which we on this side of the house approved and to which parliament gave its approval in 1957, there is no objection to this proposal; on the contrary, there is support for it.

I object to the hon. member's use of the word "now" which gives the impression that this is something the present government has done. to rectify it in a way which would accord the foresters of world war II the same status as those of world war I. I think everyone will agree that by this measure the problem is being rectified to some degree. It may be that the monetary difference will be negligible and perhaps the minister will assure me that that understanding is correct. However, there is a question of pride involved.
I know the technical arguments are all on the side of doing it the way it is being done and I readily admit this is only a sentimental argument. But in these matters no one knows better than the minister, I am sure, how important sentiment is.
There are the two anomalies, if you like. One is that the veterans of the Newfoundland forestry corps who served in world war I are regarded as veterans and those who served in world war II are not, and members of the Canadian forestry corps who served in world war II are regarded as veterans and the Newfoundlanders who served beside them doing the same job are not. I am sure that is the only point the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo was making.
We are very pleased at what is being done. We wish the government had done it last year when the War Veterans Allowance Act was amended and when this course was strongly urged upon the minister. I wish to be completely fair about it. At that time the minister said he would take it under consideration. Obviously he has taken the matter under consideration and has brought in a measure dealing with this question. I am trying to be completely fair and uncontroversial. All I am saying is that I know it would be greatly appreciated if the minister would take the additional action we are proposing.
I am going to make an appeal to the minister. We know, of course, how things are done in parliament. The bill is already drafted but all bills are susceptible of amendment with respect to phraseology particularly if no financial consideration is involved. Between the completion of the resolution stage today and our proceeding with second reading of the bill, as I presume we will very shortly, if it is not already in the bill, could the minister take another look at it and insert a form of words which would meet this sentimental consideration, if you wish to call it that, and that would satisfy the feeling of pride of the men who did such an essential job as the minister pointed out so well on Friday? Could they be given in words a recognition which would give them the feeling the Canadian Legion suggests they should have, that of being regarded as being on a basis of complete equality with other veterans.
[Mr. PickersgULJ
I do not wish to seem carping or critical. The minister will recall that when we were discussing the matter last year I said I frankly thought the Liberals should have done this when we were in office, but we did not and that is all past. If the government were to follow that course I think everyone would be happy. We would be preserving that nonpartisan, non-controversial attitude toward questions affecting our veterans which all Canadians have been proud that we have preserved steadily throughout every parliament since the end of world war II. I hope the minister can give consideration to my echo-for that is all it is-of the plea of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo who, as everyone knows, is a distinguished war veteran and who is very familiar with the feeling in this regard of the Newfoundland veterans, including the foresters.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DISALLOWANCE OF CLAIMS FOR DEDUCTIONS
REQUEST FOR DISALLOWANCE OF CLAIMS FOR DEDUCTIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of encouraging reasonable early vesting of pension rights of employees by disallowing in whole or in part the employer's claims for a deduction of the expenses Of pensions for income tax purposes where reasonable vesting provisions are not adopted.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will not read the resolution again. It is designed to promote the earlier vesting of pension rights in the various pension schemes in vogue in Canada at the present time. I realize that if all pension schemes were on a national level and operated nationally the situation would be much better. We could then have early vesting and full portability of pensions. When I put this motion on the order paper agreement with the provinces seemed to be rather remote and I have not seen anything this session that would lead me to think otherwise.
In the various pension schemes now available for employees in Canada certain things are generally true. The great majority of such schemes comprise those where employer and employee both make contributions toward the scheme. However, there are a number of union agreements where the employer makes the full contribution. I know that there are some exceptions but it is fairly generally true that the employee may recover his contributions if he terminates his work with the employer before the plan matures. It is also fairly generally true that the employee has no right to expect any part of the contributions paid into the plan on his behalf by the employer until the time of maturity is reached. This usually occurs after a period of 20 years or after an attained age or after a combination of both.
In many of these plans the employee has no claim to the part contributed by the employer if the employee's service falls short of the date of maturity by a month, a week or even a day. It has been stated, and I think there is some truth in the statement, that employers' contributions are in a sense wages withheld. The loss to an employee who is almost at retirement age would amount to some thousands of dollars, calculated on the basis of his life expectancy, if he misses out on his pension.
I am free to admit that matters of this kind come under the jurisdiction of the provinces,
(The Chairman.]
but the people of Canada subsidize these pension schemes in respect of employers' contributions to the extent of almost 50 per cent. These contributions are subsidized by reason of the fact that they are exempt from income tax and the exemption amounts to almost 50 per cent since their income tax rate is almost 50 per cent. The government grants this income tax exemption for a very worthy purpose, and if the handling of these pension funds does not meet the wishes of parliament, then I maintain that parliament has a right to withhold a part of this subsidization or even all of it unless certain conditions are met.
The resolution proposes to bring about the earlier vesting of pension rights, not by legislation which would be outside of our jurisdiction but by withholding some of the concessions granted under the Income Tax Act.
The services of employees may be terminated for many reasons. For instance, a plant may be moved. I have known of cases where plants have been moved and a number of the older employees who were near the pensionable age were left high and dry and did not receive any pension. The same thing would apply in the case of a mine. The mine might run out of ore, which often happens. The employees might be close to the pensionable age but they would get no pension.
There are various other reasons. For instance, I have known of an employee having to quit work in a plant because he developed an allergy. The plant adopted new processes involving new gases and the employee was allergic to these gases. He did not become sick but he could not continue work because of his allergy. There may be family reasons why an employee would want to move to another job. The education of his family is one example.
If earlier vesting were allowed I think this would help to make pensions portable. It would help older workers aged from 40 to 45 years to get work. If such a person applies for work at a plant at the present time, he is turned down because of his age and because he cannot pay 20 or 25 years back contributions into a pension plan. If he could take his equity to a new pension plan his chances of employment would be improved.
I am not indicating a time when there should be earlier vesting in these pension plans. It seems to me that an employee who has given a number of years of faithful service should have some vesting after ten years or even earlier. If it were done on the government level there could be vesting from the first year of service.
The government could overcome many of the injustices in private pension plans by the simple expedient of withholding these rights under the Income Tax Act. This would be a

great benefit to most of the working people of Canada engaged in industry. Circumstances can develop which can result in almost anyone being deprived of his pension. I must say that the industries in my area have been most fair. They have placed men on pension even before the maturity of their plans. On the other hand, I know of other cases where men have worked almost up to the maturity date and did not get a pension. I do not think this should be so.
I might say that another injustice in these pension plans has been brought to my attention. A number of industrial pensioners over 70 will not get the $10 increase in the old age pension which we have just provided. Many of them were placed on small industrial pensions at 65. When they reach the age of 70 their industrial pension is reduced by the amount of the old age pension and a number of these pensioners will suffer a further reduction of $10, or part of $10, in their industrial pension when we start paying them the extra $10 old age pension this month.
These people's pensions were calculated on the basis of a $40 a month old age pension; but now, when the old age pension is increased to $65, to me it does not seem quite right that they should be losing because of the increase we have granted in the old age pension. We are actually helping the pension fund, not the recipients, in these particular cases.
I do not know how many such cases there are in Canada but I am aware of a few. Our party is committed to making pensions portable. I notice the statement in the speech from the throne that an attempt would be made to secure the concurrence of the provinces in respect of certain payments, it goes on to say-
-and will take into account private pension arrangements and the need for legislation concerning portability of pension rights.
Now, it is very important to note that the letter written by the Prime Minister on January 17 to the provincial premiers sets forth certain matters but does not mention the words "portability of pensions." That appears in the speech from the throne but is not mentioned in the Prime Minister's letters. I think that, had the government the intention to go ahead with a scheme providing for portability of pensions, it should have indicated this to the premiers of the provinces. I would like to know if the government really intend doing anything about it. To me it seems so important that it should have been referred to the premiers. Personally, I do not think the government intend going ahead with it because the letter written by the Prime Minister was quite a lengthy one in connection with amending section 94A of the British
Pensions
North America Act, but did not contain any reference to portability of pensions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) for bringing this subject of portable pensions to the attention of the house. I know it is of great interest to many people in my riding and, as is well known in this house, last year the Ontario government brought in a draft bill dealing with compulsory portable pensions. The then premier of Ontario, the Hon. Leslie Frost, said he was bringing the bill in and he wished there would be the widest discussion on it by interested parties. Actually I do not agree with the hon. member for Welland

Pensions
because I think this problem of portable pensions should remain under the jurisdiction of the provinces, since the provinces are much closer to the people, and certainly contributory pensions are very close to the people.
In the House of Commons last week we had a great deal of discussion on universal pensions for all Canadians. I am inclined to think the federal government should provide the basic old age pension, plus a contributory system to the old age pension by which every citizen can contribute to it; then it should leave the problem of portable pensions to the provinces, as there are problems attached to portable pensions and many people who do not want them.
For instance, there are three words that keep cropping up in regard to portable pensions. Those three words are "mandatory, compulsory and restrictive". The Ontario draft bill states it would be compulsory for employers of 15 or more persons to establish a pension plan by 1965, meeting certain minimum standards. The draft bill also states that the pension plans would be mandatory upon all employees over 30 years of age, and it says there would be restrictions placed on refunding contributions from the employees, and that employers contributions would be vested in the employees.
When we ask governments to provide us with more and more security the inevitable result is that we chop away more and more fragments of our own freedom. Portable pensions mean that a government is forcing a man to save his own money in one particular way, and I should like to give an example of this.
A friend of mine went to work for a certain firm at the age of 20 years. When he reached his early 40's he decided he wanted to go into business for himself, and he really was not aware that the pension fund to which he had been contributing for about 19 years had refund restrictions. He thought he would be able to get about $6,000 out of the fund, $6,000 that he himself had paid into it. He found that was not so and the $6,000 he had saved had to remain in the fund. He was given a minute pension which was no use to him at all at that time and, as it subsequently turned out, he is now paying most of the pension into income tax. Hon. members may ask: what did government have to do with that particular case? Government had nothing to do with it; it was between the man and the company for which he worked. But not all pension plans have refund restrictions, and if government steps into this competitive field to make it mandatory, with regard to all pension funds,

that no employee will get his own money back, it seems to me this will create hardship for many people.
During the past two decades there has been a tremendous growth in employee-employer pension plans. Much credit goes to the unions which have negotiated wisely in this regard; much credit goes to responsible employers who have seen the wisdom of these pension plans and have used them to attract and hold good employees.
Then we must remember that some pension plans are much better than others. Some employers have shown a far higher sense of responsibility toward their employees than others, and excellent pension schemes have been built up. When government moves into these competitive fields, making them mandatory, compulsory and restrictive, almost inevitably the schemes would be reduced to the lowest denominator. I am afraid that is what would happen if the government started legislating portable pensions.
It seems to me that the perfect way to operate portable pensions would be for employers, employees and insurance companies to work out plans without government interference or legislation. By all means let us encourage portable pensions. Perhaps this resolution brought forward by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) would do that by discouraging employers through not allowing tax deductions. I think if we can encourage responsible employers, union negotiators and insurance companies to work toward portable pensions, that is the best way to do it. Let us be careful of federal government interference in what could be extremely rigid and extravagant legislation which would please no one.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take a certain amount of satisfaction in rising to support the resolution moved by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan), which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of encouraging reasonable early vesting of pension rights of employees by disallowing in whole or in part the employer's claims for a deduction of the expenses of pensions for income tax purposes where reasonable vesting provisions are not adopted.
This resolution should receive the support of hon. members on all sides of the house. It is not in any sense infringing upon anyone's personal liberty; it is simply asking the government of Canada to accept its responsibility in promoting the vesting of pensions to the advantage of the employees of corporations of this country by making certain provisions in the Income Tax Act. Throughout the years the hon. member for Welland has carried on a continuous campaign in this regard. I must

say again that I take some pleasure in having been personally associated with him in this respect.
I represent a constituency in which the largest union is the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers-who are a jolly fine lot of fellows. That union was the first one, to my knowledge, to make representations to the former government to consider income tax regulations that would provide for what was then termed the transferability of pensions. The word "portable" has since come into more general use. The Canadian Congress of Labour and other unions associated with the congress have throughout the years made representations to the former government and this government to give effect to what is the principle behind the resolution of the hon. member for Welland.
There is an interesting history to this question. The former Liberal government issued what was known as the famous blue book, which provided certain regulations with respect to the vesting of pensions. These regulations were over the signature of the former minister of national revenue, the late Dr. McCann. Apparently very little was known about these regulations until the officers of the mine, mill and smelter workers union in Trail suddenly discovered that the government of the day was not living up to its own regulations. This was brought to the attention of the government by that union, later by other unions and by members of the opposition, including supporters of the party at present in power.
As a result of those representations the minister of finance ordered an investigation. Hon. members will remember that this investigation went on for some months and representations were heard from various large corporations interested in this question. After these representations had been heard and the unions in Canada had been kept, as it were, on tip toe or in suspense for a period of months, it was finally decided that the government was not going to enforce the regulations with respect to pension vesting as found in what has now become known as the famous blue book.
However, this was a subject of such importance to emloyees that the mine, mill and smelter workers union-which represents the employees of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company in west and east Kootenay-continued to negotiate with the company in an effort to get the company to recognize the principle of transferable or portable pensions in its agreement with the union. They did this because, without the vesting of pensions the employee has no vested right in the pension and is almost affixed to his employment until he receives
Pensions
his pension rights in the ordinary course of events. The vesting of pensions makes it possible for employees to have a certain mobility. If they wish to move, for family, health or other reasons, they will not lose all they have invested in a pension fund by virtue of discontinuing their employment with a certain corporation or company.
In this respect the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company was the first large corporation in Canada to include pension vesting in an agreement with the union which represented the employees. So the workers employed by the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company have the right, on attaining age 50 and after 20 years service with the company, to have their pension payable to them when they reach retirement age whether or not they are employed by Cominco. This means they can sever their employment with the company, go to work for any other company, and they still have a vested right in their pension. They can sever their employment for any reason whatsoever without losing their pension rights. This pension plan also allows an employee with 25 years service, regardless of his age, to commute his pension to the benefit of his wife. This agreement brought to a successful conclusion some years of negotiation between the union and the company to achieve these ends.
While this right has been obtained by the employees of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company as a result of bargaining between the bargaining agent of the union and the company, the employees of that company are still not satisfied that this is the final answer to the question. The employees of the company, although they enjoy rights not enjoyed by most other employees of large corporations in Canada, want to see this right obtained as a result of law, as a result of the federal government accepting certain responsibility, and not only as a result of negotiation and bargaining.
I am sure the present government is fully acquainted with the situation. I notice the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell), parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) is taking a great interest in what hon. members opposite him have to say on these matters and I have no doubt he is fully acquainted with all the circumstances surrounding this question of pension vesting and with the arguments which have been put forward by the unions, by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan), the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) and other members of this house. We trust he will be favourably influenced by the arguments put forward on this occasion.

Pensions
However, we must emphasize that we support this resolution applying to private pension plans as the first step in the establishment of a national pension plan. Pending the introduction of such a plan we urge the government to accept some responsibility in developing pension vesting, and in promoting the idea of pension vesting by recognizing it in certain regulations relating to the Income Tax Act. We in this group have always urged the solution as being a national pension scheme. We notice there is mention of such a scheme in the speech from the throne this year and we are delighted to know that this small group to which I belong has had a favourable influence on the government at an expedient moment. We are looking forward to the introduction of legislation concerning a national pension plan and we hope we shall hear the details of such a plan prior to dissolution, so that we may know exactly what the government has in mind. Possibly, in view of the great interest the hon. member for Carleton takes in this subject he will give us a hint, or at least some intimation, of the benefits which are to flow from the sentence in the speech from the throne which has aroused our anticipation with respect to a national pension plan. I can see the hon. member is sitting anxiously in his seat waiting for the moment when he can have something to say on this subject.
