I am not surprised to find those who sit on your immediate left following each other with such enthusiasm on behalf of state intervention in a matter which is primarily a personal matter. I am the first to concede that there are problems which will arise, as the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) has pointed out, when people who are almost within sight of receiving a pension are disqualified from doing so for one reason or another, possibly missing it by a day or by a week. I think that is something which should cause us concern in this parliament as a state of affairs which we should naturally seek to remedy.
I am not sure that by using the stick of the state to beat malefactors we are going to achieve the result sought by the hon. member for Welland. I used the phrase "the stick of the state", but the hon. member put it
[Mr. Herridge.l
in more eloquent language by suggesting that the problem would be solved by disallowing in whole or in part an employer's claims for a deduction of the expenses of pensions for income tax purposes where reasonable vesting provisions are not adopted. This means that parliament would be asked to intervene, as he puts it, in pension arrangements between employers and employees-to be, as it were, an arbitrator and to hold a penalty over the heads of employers who do not give their employees reasonable vesting facilities.
The first thought that comes to my mind is that one of the parties to a pension plan, the employer, has a contractual obligation, and the other, the employee, has a contractual right. These are usually hammered out in the form of a lengthy document held by the trustee to whom the pension payments are made. Surely, if there is any question involving a hiatus of time-a case of an employee who fails to qualify by a day, a week, or even a few months-there should be some provision in the contract for its solution. For example, there might be provision in the contract for the appointment for an impartial board of arbitration whose members would comprise somebody appointed by the employer, somebody appointed by the employee and, perhaps, a third party agreed on by both. This board could then consider the justice or injustice of the employee's claim.
Surely, what we have in the present proposal contains a suggestion of the big stick -the suggestion that the state must intervene because other remedies are useless. Perhaps the state should, indeed, intervene if no other way around the problem can be found. But it would not be a parliamentary intervention. We would simply be setting wheels in motion, if we pass this resolution, and putting the proposal into legislation which would then become a matter for bureaucratic interpretation. I do not use the word "bureaucratic" as a colourful adjective or in any invidious sense whatsoever. But when one is dealing with such an important matter as the Income Tax Act he has to be extremely careful. It is necessary to spell out rights and obligations in endless detail in regulations and memoranda so that there is as little discretionary right as possible left with the civil servants who will be applying these regulations, and so that decisions may be laid down as far as possible within the four corners of the regulations themselves.
I point this out because I think it indicates a serious defect in the approach made to this question by the hon. member for Welland. I do not quarrel with the hon. member's intention, but I point out that it would not be for parliament to spell out the regulations

designed to see whether an employer was acting justly or unjustly. Rather, it would be for the Department of National Revenue to control this aspect of the situation. In short I am asking: can regulations ensure justice, or is there a possibility that some other means can be found of achieving the objects which the hon. member for Welland has in mind. As I say, I do not quarrel with the end the hon. member seeks to achieve; I quarrel with the way in which he would go about obtaining it.
The question of the portability of pensions was raised in the debate this afternoon. The hon. member said he thought pensions would be made more portable if this resolution were adopted. I followed him anxiously at that point because I had some reservations about this matter and I regret to say the hon. gentleman has not dispelled the reservations I hold.
The hon. member said, for example, that older men and women would have a better chance of employment. I believe that was the spirit of what he said. The employment of older people is a serious matter, of course, and if the hon. member's suggestion is correct we would hasten to accept the remedy. But as I look at the situation I think the hon. member's resolution would result in there being rather less chances of employment for these people, because in its final form the resolution really means a person instead of accepting his pension at age 65 or 70, let us say, under certain conditions would be entitled to receive it at an earlier age. It seems to me this could very well lead to employers being hesitant about employing older people who, instead of continuing in employment for 10 or 15 years, might work for only five or 10 and then seek early vesting of their pension rights.
I may be wrong and I hope I am-

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to support this resolution. I hasten to dissociate myself from the two extremely reactionary and negative interjections made by the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) and the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave). To say that this resolution proposes the "big stick" idea is just nonsense.
The state has granted to some people the privilege of deducting from taxable income certain amounts under certain conditions, and now upon examination it is found that this often does not work to the advantage of either the state or many of the individuals concerned. The time has come for a reexamination. It is not a question of bureaucracy nor of state imposition. Quite contrary to what was suggested by the hon. member for York-Humber it is a case of liberating citizens, of giving them back their rights, of allowing them to do what is in their own best interests. It is in this spirit that the resolution is put forward.

I do not know what my hon. friend is referring to, in detail, Mr. Speaker, but if he will send me a short resume of what it is to which he refers I shall be glad to answer his question later, if time permits.
The portability of pensions is one of the most urgent of the new problems facing us as an industrial nation. I describe it as a new problem for this reason. Industrial pension plans were put into effect for a purpose. They were designed to fill a need at the time. The purpose was to provide security for workers in their mature years and after retirement. But the nature of the plans has created new problems not envisaged at the time they were established. Some people wish to leave their employment before the

age of retirement. The mover of the resolution has cited some of the reasons why people wish to do so from time to time. Other persons are laid off before they are entitled to vesting privileges.
They are the losers. The only people who gain are those who stick it out until the end, those who remain until the age of retirement. The approach to the company pension plan depends on what hat you are wearing. From the standpoint of industry its purpose, to an extent at least, is to make it difficult for valuable employees to leave their employment. A pension plan becomes in a sense a ball and chain to a particular firm. An existing plan has same advantages for management and for some long term employees who remain until retirement. However, there are disadvantages for both management and employees and these are very substantial ones.
Management sometimes keeps on staff an employee who has grown stale and has lost interest in his job, and this is done because he is near the retirement age. Not all management is that altruistic but there have been many cases in which this was done. It is also true that management is unable to hire new employees of mature years. Many potential employees who have great skill and who are settled in their habits cannot be hired because their hiring would upset the actuarial soundness of pension plans.
From the employees' standpoint pension plans are equally unsatisfactory, if not more so, except of course for those who remain in the same employment until retirement. Unemployed workers are barred from employment because of age. Mature workers who want only the right to work are denied that right. To my hon. friends opposite I say this. In the last few months I have interviewed many individuals who are not old by ordinary standards. I refer to persons of age 40 years to 45 years. Some of them have sought employment in every major industry in the To-ronto-Oshawa-Hamilton area and have been turned down because of their age. I ask my hon. friends this question: Is this liberty? Is this freedom? Is it right that a 40 year old Canadian should be barred at the door of a large industry because his employment would upset the actuarial soundness of a plan which is a privilege granted by this parliament of Canada? Is that what they call freedom? I do not think it is.
Employees are denied the right to move from job to job for their own betterment. People learn from experience. The broader his experience, the more proficient and valuable a person becomes. Company pension plans restrict the movement of labour as do other plans, as a matter of fact, such as

the civil service and education board pension plans. I am one of those who believe that it would be good for many civil servants to take a two year sabbatical leave once or twice during their lifetime and to seek employment in industry. When they return to the civil service I am sure that they would be much more valuable and experienced persons; that their perspectives would be better and that they would be better able to see both sides of a problem and to gauge more accurately the relative merits of suggestions made to them by industry and commerce.
If school teachers could leave teaching for a year or two at least once or twice during their careers and accept other employment, I think they would gain from the breadth of knowledge that would then be available to them. I believe they would become more valuable, experienced, knowledgeable and understanding teachers than they were before they had the advantage of this outside experience. This statement applies as well to clergymen and others.
At the present time those who participate in retirement plans are denied the right to do this as, should they leave their employment, they lose their pension rights in most cases. This is a restriction which I think is a disadvantage. The desirability of mobility is real and the advantage of mobility is real. If this is so, as I maintain it is, portability should not be confined to provincial boundaries.
The question of jurisdiction has been raised. Whether or not this is a matter which falls entirely within the competence of the provinces is a matter of opinion. Some people think it is such a matter. Other people think that it is not such a matter. If it lies within the competence of the provinces, I think a constitutional amendment should be sought. My hon. friend from York-Humber made reference to the Frost plan which was widely discussed last year. However, in the opinion of many people the Frost plan was too narrow, too restrictive and would not accomplish the purposes which must be accomplished. I think it would be better-

should be recognized as veterans. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps you would permit me to depart from the usual practice in speaking on such resolutions to deal very briefly with an event which I am sure has touched every member of this house who has been interested in the veterans over the years. I refer to the passing of Judith Robinson, a remarkable and distinguished member of the press gallery, an accomplished critic and a great Canadian but above all a person who fought throughout the years for the rights of veterans, particularly the pensioners and those entitled to war veterans allowance.
I should like to pay tribute to her not only for her qualities of excellence in her journalistic career, not only because I counted her a friend, as so many others did, but primarily on behalf of her special friends, the veterans of Canada, especially the veterans of world war I who received her constant help and encouragement. She fought for them during all her adult life in the tradition of her father before her. As all hon. members will recall, she learned of their problems from her father and from others with whom she came in contact. After the passing of her father she carried on the battle in a never-ending crusade for the betterment of the lot of the veterans. I think everyone in the house will join with me in saying that not only was she a good writer of the highest integrity, an incisive critic, a devotee of democracy and a watchdog of the rights of the people in parliament but she also held a special place in the heart of the veterans. The memory of this fighting lady from the Toronto Telegram still holds that warm place in their hearts.
I should like to deal now with some of the remarks that have been made during the course of the debate on the resolution now before us. When I first came to Ottawa as the member for Saskatoon I roomed with the hon. member for St. John's East, a Newfoundlander. Our association was productive of many interesting exchanges. One of the first things we discussed, he being a very young man, was the general position of

veterans in Canada, and in particular the position of veterans and others in Newfoundland who had served their country. I remember discussing with the hon. member for St. John's East during the years 1957 and 1958 the question of the Newfoundland foresters and how something might be done to give recognition to the contribution they had made in defence of what is now part of Canada. On this occasion I should like to pay tribute to the work he has done, and also to that of the Solicitor General. These two gentlemen have been responsible for a great deal of my education in regard to Newfoundland and, over the years, I think we have undertaken certain joint ventures that have resulted and will result in benefits to Newfoundlanders as well as to the country as a whole.
In dealing with this particular aspect of what is broadly called the veterans charter, I believe we should pay tribute to those who have taken the time and occasion in years gone by to further the cause of those particular persons who are mentioned in this resolution brought in for the benefits available under the War Veterans Allowance Act by virtue of the resolution that included them under the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act.
In reply to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate I may say that there will be no distinction between these, the classes brought under the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act in regard to the allowances they receive, and the others under the War Veterans Allowance Act. As with all items of the veterans charter these, I believe, are noncontroversial pieces of legislation. They are outside the realm of party controversy.
From time to time since 1958 the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo has mentioned the foresters. I think it is perhaps fair to say that with the change of government there has been this interest shown for the first time as evidenced by this resolution, in rectifying a number of the anomalies that have existed in legislating for benefits for those who helped in the defence of the country. Ever since this government took office there has been an extensive and continuous review of the various items of legislation which make up the veterans charter. Now that we have reached this particular item, the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act, I am very glad to say it is possible to provide for the inclusion of the world war I Canadian merchant marine and the group of Canadians who served in the Canadian merchant services of the allies, the world war II Canadian merchant marine and the group of Canadians who served with Canada's allies on certified non-Canadian

ships, as well as the world war II group of civilian firefighters who had service in the United Kingdom.
In regard to the latter group, if I may again say a word in reminiscence, I had no sooner been elected in Saskatoon than I received representations on behalf of this particular group. The Canadian firefighters asked for their inclusion in this legislation and I am glad this has now been achieved. Then also there are the groups of world war I and world war II voluntary aid detachments and world war II overseas welfare workers, world war II Canadian civilian aircrew of the Royal Air Force transport command, in addition to the Newfoundland overseas foresters unit.
I have a particular interest in the civilian air crew of the R.A.F. transport command, as it later became known. It was originally known as the R.A.F. ferry command. While serving with the R.C.A.F. I was seconded for most of the war to the R.A.F. and served for some time with the R.A.F. ferry command, and later with the R.A.F. transport command, originally based in Dorval and later overseas. Many of the gentlemen who took part as civilians in that gigantic operation of getting aircraft from the new world to the old, aircraft that were in serviceable form to take part in the defence of Britain and later Africa-these gentlemen came from all walks of life and were a most amazing and interesting collection. They had been barn-stormers, civilian air line pilots, or persons who had taken wireless navigation in their spare time.
They came to Montreal in the early days of the war and there embarked on the trip across the North Atlantic which, in the aircraft of that time, was quite a formidable venture. It is interesting to note that the fatal casualty rate of that group was something like 22 per cent and most of the fatalities occurred not from enemy action but from weather, engine failures, mechanical defects and things of that sort. It was quite a high ratio and in my particular group the ratio was 25 per cent killed.
Those of us who were in the air force had the protection of the veterans charter but those who were civilians, although they were paid well at that time, had none of that protection. I am very, very pleased it has been possible to have those gentlemen included under this particular act. I thought it might be interesting to place on the record some of the efforts that had been made to achieve this, I have a summary, covering the highlights of the representations and negotiations carried out over a period of two and a half years following world war II between the Canadian and British governments to secure veterans status for civilians in the wartime transport command.

The first step was the presentation of a brief to the first parliamentary committee on veterans affairs on October 29, 1945. Then on November 6, 1955, Joe Weaver and Jack Pierce appeared as witnesses before the committee. Several cabinet ministers, including the then minister of veterans affairs, Mr. Mackenzie, were present. After the meeting several members from all parties congratulated the delegates and said theirs was the finest presentation they had heard before the committee. Now, in 1962, we are able to implement some of the recommendations made at that time.
The group persisted and in February, 1946, they again presented a brief before the interdepartmental committee on veterans affairs, meeting in camera. On March 26, 1946, that committee issued its report reviewing the whole history of ferry command and the position of civilian aircrew in it. This report was very favourable to the civilian members of the ferry command.
On May 14, 1946, the subject was referred to a subcommittee under the chairmanship of Leslie Mutch, a member of parliament at that time. On July 8, 1946, the subcommittee reported to the special committee in the following terms-
-recommending unanimously the introduction of a bill to provide all the principal benefits and grants to former civilian flying personnel of the R.A.F. ferry command... your subcommittee felt that an organization which had lost 22 per cent of its members dead, and as near as we could discover whose casualties were somewhere between 90 and 100 persons killed, has certainly made a contribution which was comparable to the contribution made by other organizations of a wholly civilian nature which have received benefits under veterans' legislation...
The subcommittee expressed itself strongly in regard to these people. Again, on July 23, 1946 the committee's recommendations were incorporated in the twenty second report to the house, and so the history went. But the civilian members of ferry command have had to wait until now to get this recognition of the service they performed.
I might say that they flew to all places in the world. They flew all sorts of aircraft. I can remember flying across the Atlantic in an aircraft, and in order for it to carry enough gas to reach the other side a tank which filled the entire cabin of the aircraft had to be constructed. Other aircraft flew across the Atlantic with great belly tanks slung underneath. These strange adaptations which had to be made to the aircraft to get them to fighting fronts resulted in the casualties and deaths to which I have been referring.
Mr. Chairman, a number of other hon. members would like to speak in regard to this resolution and, I feel sure, support it. The

Civilian War Pensions
Minister of Veterans Affairs, when he was dealing earlier with some of the remarks which had been made by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, emphasized-and I think in closing I should repeat it-that with regard to the Newfoundland foresters the progress which is represented by the incorporation of these foresters under this legislation is real progress; it is progress which has been asked for by the foresters since 1949, if my memory serves me correctly. Though its initial annual cost is relatively limited-$60,000-it is estimated that the annual cost will tend to increase and improve in five years after the present amendment is made and will reach a figure of something in the order of $1,200,000. It should be a real benefit to those members of the Newfoundland overseas forestry unit who served and were requested to stay in their units as members of the forestry corps despite their inclinations to become members of the armed forces.
I think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will agree with the correctness of this statement, that the Newfoundland foresters, though they originally made contracts for six months only, were subsequently required to sign on for the duration and in each contract there was a covenant requiring that the man would not join the armed forces or transfer to them.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this resolution to amend the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act. When the minister introduced this resolution on Friday he enumerated seven different classes of people who had served in world war I or world war II and who would come under the legislation to be provided by the bill when it is introduced. In general I endorse the proposal the minister made to this committee and I think we will know more exactly what is to be done when the bill is presented to the house following the adoption of the resolution. I do, however, think it might have been better if these men and women had been recognized under the veterans charter rather than under this particular act.
For a number of years now we have argued in this chamber in favour of benefits for the merchant marine. My hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo last Friday gave a very apt description of the dangers through which they went during world war I and world war II, and indeed one cannot minimize the contribution they made in two world wars nor the extent of the dangers they faced. Undoubtedly their contribution to the war effort played no small part in the final outcome and I believe they are entitled to all the benefits which might accrue to members of any other branch of the services.

In this amendment we have also recognized the Newfoundland foresters. This was a unit formed on November 18, 1939, just a few weeks after the outbreak of war. The final enlistment amounted to 3,680 men. Newfoundlanders enlisted in this particular branch of the services because they were encouraged to do so. Almost a year ago now, on February 7, 1961 when we were discussing the Pension Act I gave a brief history of the Newfoundland foresters unit. At that time I was able to place on the record information which would substantiate the claim that these men were encouraged to join the forestry unit. For the first nine months of the war men who joined this unit were under contract for six months. After the first nine months they were under contract for the duration and were not permitted to join any other branch of the services.
They believed then that they were serving in an area where they could make their best contribution. Also, they were members of a unit in which they had been encouraged to enlist by the then commission government of Newfoundland under instructions from the home office in London. We have now arrived at the position in veterans legislation where Newfoundland foresters of world war I are considered to be veterans; Canadian foresters of world war I are considered to be veterans; Canadian foresters of world war II are considered to be veterans; but Newfoundland foresters of world war II are not considered to be veterans under the veterans charter. Here I think there is a significant difference. However, the amendments to the present act form a real step forward and I hope we are not too far away from the time when Canadian veterans will be considered because of the contribution they made under perilous conditions and not because of any legal technicalities in the legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to enter this debate very briefly. First of all, I think the government in general and the Minister of Veterans Affairs in particular should be especially commended for this particular measure. I am sure that when the history of these parliaments is written Colonel Brooks and the present minister will go down as two of the finest ministers of veterans affairs parliament has ever known.
I was interested to hear the minister's remarks about the merchant marine, the fire fighters and the Newfoundland foresters. The merchant marine rendered most valuable service on all the seas of the world. I do not suppose too many hon. members of the committee know that the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, who is away this day

on business, served in world war II for over five years in practically every ocean as a member of the merchant marine. He served in this force because he was of low medical category, even though he tried many times to enlist in Canada's army.
The minister said he thought there might be only a few hundred survivors left out of the 5,000 who served. I was rather surprised to hear that out of 5,000 men who served between 1940 and 1945 there should only be two or three hundred left at this point. Perhaps the minister will later give a word of explanation about that. The firefighters are another group which especially deserves to be given recognition. These men served in England through much of the heavy bombing. I am interested in this because for a short time I was attached as a Canadian army officer to the firefighting service in Great Britain in the second world war.
I should like to speak briefly about the Newfoundland forestry unit. Over the last two or three years the case of these men has been pressed strongly, especially by the Newfoundland members, who I think should be commended for their zeal. I think that here again the government has shown a high degree of generosity. After all, between 1945 and 1949 the government of the United Kingdom did nothing for these men. Nothing was done in 1949 under the terms of union, either, and I often wonder why that was so. I wish the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo were here; perhaps he could answer that- I am sure he could. Again, nothing was done between 1949 and 1957, and that is significant.
I do take objection to statements which have been made by my good friends the hon. members for Kootenay West and Burin-Burgeo contending there was no distinction between the Canadian forestry corps of world wars I and II, and the Newfoundland foresters. There was the greatest distinction inasmuch as the Canadian forestry corps of world wars I and II were soldiers of the Canadian army and as such were liable for service anywhere in the world. Many were men with several decorations from the first world war. They were members of the Canadian army and as such they could be assigned to service anywhere. As a matter of fact, when 8,000 Canadian foresters in the second world war were stationed in northern Scotland beside the Newfoundland foresters, every month so many of them were requested to transfer to the units in southern England, in Sicily and in Italy. A great many did go, and many became casualties. I do object to the statement that the Newfoundland foresters were not
Civilian War Pensions
permitted to transfer. Perhaps that is so up to a point, but I know of several cases where foresters in northern Scotland transferred to the Canadian army and then went on to serve in southern England and in different theatres of war. The Canadian forestry corps sent one forestry battalion to France and these men took part in the Ardennes fighting where they sustained a number of casualties. There is a distinct difference between the forestry unit of Newfoundland in the second world war and the Canadian forestry corps. This Conservative government has been extremely generous and I hope the people of Newfoundland, when the time does come, will recognize the generosity of the present Minister of Veterans Affairs and of this government, in this particular measure.

This is one subject which does not require lengthy debate because everyone is in favour of the resolution which will permit the payment of allowances to surviving former members of a number of Canadian organizations who made an outstanding voluntary contribution to the war effort during two world wars.
On previous occasions I have advocated the principle that those who volunteered for service, no matter in what capacity, whether as foresters, firemen or seamen in the merchant marine, should, together with their dependents, be recognized as eligible for pensions under the Veterans Allowance Act. In many cases it was through no fault of these men that they were diverted from service in a theatre of war. Their services were channelled into jobs considered by the government of the day to be in the best interest of the war effort at that time, and for this reason they found themselves in services which did not qualify them for veterans benefits.
Let us consider, for instance, the case of the men who served in the merchant marine. They suffered hardships in the course of their work equal to if not greater than those experienced in any of the combat force units. I am thinking especially of those who were assigned to convoys and ships on the North sea running up through the Arctic circle in waters where their ships were in constant danger of torpedo attack. Then there are the firefighters who volunteered to go to Britain to help hard pressed London during the great blitz and who were in constant danger during the performance of their duty.
The establishing of eligibility for assistance under the act has long been overdue. Nevertheless I congratulate the minister for recognizing the need now; delated though his action may be, it will meet with the approval of the Canadian people.

Civilian War Pensions
Those men who served overseas in the forestry units from the lakehead area will appreciate being considered as veterans in every respect. A couple of years ago the Canadian Legion adopted at its convention a resolution which gave these men the privilege of membership in the Canadian Legion as veterans. This applies with equal force to the forestry unit from Newfoundland on whose behalf the hon. members for Humber-St. George's and Burin-Burgeo have made appeals in the past.
Last year and the year before, as a member of the committee on veterans affairs, I was impressed by the several briefs which were presented to the committee by various veterans organizations and more so by the restraint and logic which the delegations showed in their presentations. I wish to congratulate them on their responsibility on behalf of their members.
Canada has reason to be proud of her young men and women who offered their services to their country in times of conflict, endured hardships and faced the horrible consequences of war without asking reasons why. I have always felt that our duty is never to let down those who may now find themselves in need of assistance-an assistance which I do not for one moment consider as charity but, rather, as something which is their just due from a grateful country.
The recognition granted to the second world war overseas welfare workers serving in the Red Cross, the St. John Ambulance brigade, and the Scottish ministry of health, as well as to Canadian civilian crews of the Royal Air Force transport command, merits the support of every member, and I am sure it will also receive the general approval of all Canadians.
In short, this is good legislation and should not be subject to political partisanship.

The last words of the hon. member for Fort William, when he stated that this measure should not be subject to political partisanship are words I heartily agree with. The hon. member for Humber-St. George's, the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and the hon. member for Fort William himself have all spoken strongly, with a great Liberal tradition behind them which means, in effect: let us not do anything about it until we have to, but if we have to, let us speak in favour of it.
Let me say that this Conservative government in the last five years, in making the veterans charter and in improving pensions and veterans allowances all down the line, has shown a lead which cannot be duplicated in the history of this parliament; it is second to none. The hon. member for Humber-St.

George's states that he and his friends have advocated for many years a measure of the kind now under consideration, and the other day the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo stated that for some time he and others in his party-and I cannot help reiterate that it is the Liberal party-had advocated such a move. Advocacy is not enough. It remained for the Conservative party to wrap up veterans legislation, amend it and put it on a sound basis.
Before leaving the contributions made by the hon. members for Burin-Burgeo, Humber-St. George's and Fort William, let me say that in my opinion politics have nothing to do with this important question. Over the years in the standing committee on veterans affairs these hon. gentlemen in no uncertain terms have voiced their opinions. They have advocated the introduction of legislative amendments such as those foreshadowed by the present resolution. To my mind there is no question concerning the sincerity of these hon. gentlemen. For that reason I said politics are not involved. Unfortunately, however, the party to which the hon. gentlemen belong has seen fit to take little action with respect to improvements in veterans legislation. The words they use in advocating these improvements do not mean very much.
In my submission the present Minister of Veterans Affairs and the previous minister, Senator Brooks, deserve much more commendation than they are receiving from hon. gentlemen in the opposition parties in this house. The former and the present minister have done a good job and let us never forget that. Their work on behalf of veterans does not date back only to 1957. My reading of the reports of the standing committee on veterans affairs indicates that these hon. gentlemen speaking on behalf of the Conservative party have long advocated that veterans legislation be improved. The Conservative party has always stood for improved veterans legislation and now that it has assumed power it is losing no time in introducing improvements.
World war II ended in 1946. Between 1946 and 1957, the year in which the Liberal party was defeated, we did not see brought forward improvements to veterans legislation, despite what had been advocated by hon. members of the Liberal party. The Liberal party did not see fit to place on the statute books of Canada amendments to our veterans charter.
An examination of the resolution will indicate that seven categories of persons are covered. I shall not restate them as the minister enlarged on this subject in his address. However, let me make this point.

The legislation foreshadowed by this resolution will, to a great extent, button up veterans legislation. It will indicate that we appreciate the contribution made in the last war by our veterans and all allied personnel.
The recognition now accorded to Canada's merchant seamen is of importance as is that accorded all other categories of persons dealt with. An examination of the reports of the standing committee on veterans affairs over the years will reveal that what is being brought forward by this resolution has been in the minds of hon. members of the Conservative party for many years.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS PROVIDING FOR EXTENSION OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
This resolution, Mr. Chairman, deals with another important act in the veterans charter. This particular act has been in effect since July 1, 1953. It was intended to provide opportunities for advanced education to a child of a member of the forces who lost his life while on service during world war II, or afterwards from a cause deemed to be related to his wartime service, or
Civilian War Pensions
directly attributable to subsequent peacetime service. The children of those who died during the campaign in Korea, or as a result thereof, are also eligible. It was hoped that by this means children would be able to enjoy the academic advantages which their fathers would have endeavoured to give them had they lived.
When the original studies were made it was anticipated that perhaps 1,100 to 1,200 students in all would obtain benefits consisting of allowances payable during the academic year and the payment of annual fees up to a maximum of $500 a year.
The number of children assisted under the act has greatly exceeded the original estimate. Up to December 31 last, 2,541 applications have been approved. Of these students, 694 have completed their courses and 962 are now in training. The most popular university courses have proven to be arts and science, in which 358 students have completed their courses or are still in attendance, and in the field of education, where 309 students have graduated or are now pursuing a course. Large numbers have also enrolled for courses in engineering and applied science, and in commerce and business administration. Numbers of others are in such courses as medicine, theology, social work and agriculture. Over 350 have either completed their courses or are in training in the field of nursing.
This act has thus proven to be a most useful piece of veterans legislation, both for the families it was intended to help and for the country.
The present amendments proposed in the bill are primarily intended to give effect to the government's wish to provide assistance on the basis of the increased expenditures which are now required and to enable to completion of courses which are now cut short because of the limits at present imposed on maximum age and length of period of assistance.
The rate of allowances payable has been in the nature of a supplement to the pension a child receives because of the parent's death. The original allowance was $25 a month during each academic year. In September, 1958 the act was amended to increase the allowance to $60 a month to an entitled student over age 21 where his pension had ceased at that age, thus providing a continuing total income comparable to that received during the period pension was payable. It is only proper that, following the pension increases of last year, the allowances should be amended to keep pace. While a child is in receipt of a pension an additional monthly allowance of $25 is payable during the academic year. When the pension ceases, however, the additional monthly allowance now provided, $35,
794	HOUSE OF
Children of War Dead Act means that the total monthly income of the child is reduced from $79 to $60. It is now proposed to increase the allowance under this act so that when pension ceases the total income during the academic year is not affected. The annual total cost of this amendment is estimated at $71,000.
At present the act provides for a maximum period of assistance of 36 months or four academic years, and further that assistance may not be granted beyond the academic year in which the student attains age 25. A number of cases have come to attention in which a meritorious student has embarked upon a sound educational program requiring university training exceeding four years, such as a course in law or medicine. It does not seem right that such a student should be cut off from assistance while he is only part way through his course and shows promise of being able scholastically to complete it with distinction. It is therefore proposed that the minister have discretion to authorize the extension of the period during which assistance may be granted so that such a student may continue to receive assistance until the completion of an approved course of study which will lead to a definite goal.
There have also been a number of instances in which, through a combination of circumstances, students have been unable to commence their courses, usually for health or economic reasons, by age 21, as at present is generally required. It is therefore proposed, where circumstances warrant, to permit such a student to be enrolled under this act.
Where a student has been delayed in commencing or continuing this higher education it is further proposed to permit him to receive assistance, where these special circumstances and his progress warrant, up to the end of the academic year in which he attains age 30. It is evident that such exceptions to the general principle have considerable merit, as they will enable both the student and this country to benefit to the full from the career for which he is preparing.
There are two or three clarifications proposed in the section of the act defining a student in order to enable assistance to be granted to a number who seem to fall within the original intention of the legislation but through technicalities in the present definition are excluded. These are comparatively small groups who are deprived of benefits because of early marriage or the death of the parent after his married child became 21 years of age. There are one or two other amendments of an administrative nature needed to clarify and simplify the definition of student and the arrangement of the schedule.
That, Mr. Chairman, is an outline of what is intended in the bill which will follow this

resolution. It is obvious from the figures I have given that the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act has been very successful. I think that parliament and former members of the House of Commons who were responsible for this measure may feel quite pleased that 2,500 orphan children have been assisted through this particular act, which has provided the means for them to pursue higher education which would not normally have been available to them.
When one considers the various courses through which they have been passing, and the fact that they do not receive their allowances unless they prove they are capable of continuing the courses, hon. members will appreciate that this has been a very useful piece of legislation, and it is only fitting that orphan children of those who have lost their lives in the defence of our country should receive this type of help. It is only the type of help which, had their fathers lived, they perhaps would have obtained through parental resources, but handicapped by the loss of a parent they then become wards of the state in this connection and I think it is highly creditable to Canada that this provision has been made for these children.

the second reading of Bill No. C-36 to amend the War Service Grants Act.
He said: The purpose of this bill and the following one which we are to consider, and the bill which I hope to bring in very soon dealing with the Veterans Land Act, is to extend the date of the termination of these acts until 1968.
This one in particular, the War Service Grants Act, was passed during the session of 1944-45 for the purpose of providing veterans and certain dependants with war service gratuities and re-establishment credits. The amounts were based on the length of service and depended on whether service was
79G

War Service Grants Act in this country or outside the western hemisphere. The benefits of the act are also available to those who took part in the campaign in Korea.
Up to December 31, 1961 the gratuities which were paid because of service during world war II amounted to a total of $470,056,000 and the total paid on account of special force service in Korea amounted to $6,695,000. The last annual report of the department, which was tabled the other day, shows that during the fiscal year 1960-61 nearly $10,000 in world war II gratuities were paid and about $900 arising from the action in Korea. The recent experience of the department indicates that there are still a number of veterans both of world war II and Korea who have not yet applied for their gratuities. The present deadline for the receipt of applications for gratuities is September 30 of this year.
Up to December 31,	1961 a total of
$309,369,000 world war II re-establishment credits has been paid and $3,704,000 as a result of service in Korea. At that time there were still 65,475 world war II veterans who had not received all of their credit, the outstanding total of which amounted to $10,264,000, an average amount of some $157. There were still 2,098 veterans with service in Korea who had an outstanding amount of credit of some $314,000. The present period during which a world war II veteran may apply for his credit expires on September 30, 1962 while the period available to a veteran Of Korea expires in 1968. The department has found that for the nine months ending December 31, 1961 there were 12,478 world war II credits approved for a total of $1,367,000 and during the same period 834 credits payable because of service in Korea were made available for a total of some $67,000. It is thus apparent that unless the period during which credits are available is extended, a great many veterans will not have a suitable opportunity to use their credits wisely or, indeed, will not be able to use them at all.
The major proposal contained in this bill is, therefore, the extension of the period during which application may be made for unpaid war service gratuity and outstanding re-establishment credit.
It is proposed to extend the period in each instance as it relates both to service during world war II or during the campaign in Korea, until October 31, 1968. Such an extended period should give an ample opportunity for the comparatively small number of veterans who have not yet received their war service gratuities to apply for them and provide sufficient time for the much larger


group of veterans to decide on the best way in which their remaining credit can be usefully employed.
Another amendment, which is of a technical nature, would allow veterans who have had their re-establishment credits frozen because of an application for benefits under the Veterans Land Act to have one year after the application is withdrawn or their qualification cancelled in which to apply for the use of their credits. At present such a one year period is available only where a contract has been actually made with the director and subsequently terminated. The effect of this amendment will, of course, not be felt until the normal period of availability expires, but will at that time prove to be a most useful provision.
There are also a few administrative amendments, two of which relate to the reservation of re-establishment credit for specific purposes; that is, the payment of premiums on veterans insurance and as a condition of qualification under the Veterans Land Act.
In summing up, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill before the house is to extend the terminal date to October 31, 1968.

Mr. Speaker, I will speak briefly on second reading of this bill after listening to the minister's explanatory remarks.
As one who was a member of the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs in 1945, I think it is interesting to note that after a period of 17 years we are amending an act which has proved most successful. Toward the conclusion of world war II committees of both the federal and provincial governments gave some study and consideration to the rehabilitation of veterans returning from the war. Veterans organizations often discussed this matter in their branches and at provincial and federal conventions and subsequently made representations to the government. I remember clearly the myriad suggestions put forward at that time by organizations and persons who were seriously concerned with the introduction of sound legislation that would work to the advantage of veterans whose welfare was being considered.
I think it must be with some degree of satisfaction that hon. members who were in the house at that time look back to the period over which this act has been in operation. It requires very minor amendments today.
We are pleased the government of that day accepted some of the recommendations put forward by parliamentary committees and advanced by veterans organizations. If I remember correctly the bill was a composite of the large number of suggestions made. I

am sure it is correct to say that the government through this act pioneered an entirely new approach to the question of veterans rehabilitation.
I am glad the act is to be extended to October 31, 1968. On a number of occasions we have advanced the date of application of an act a few years and an amending bill had to be introduced extending it another two or three years. I think it is wise to take one bite of the cherry in dealing with legislation of this type instead of adopting a piecemeal approach.
The extended date will provide ample time for all those coming within the terms of the legislation to secure the benefits to which they are entitled.

He said: The Veterans Insurance Act became effective in February, 1945. It provides an opportunity to secure life insurance protection with a very low medical standard. It was designed particularly to enable veterans who had lost insurability during world war II to provide an insurance estate.
Insurance is also available to widows of those who died on service during the war. It is also available to merchant seamen who were eligible to receive a special bonus or a war service bonus.
The benefits of the act have been extended to those who saw service in Korea, and their widows.
The original period of eligibility expired three years after discharge from service or the effective date of the act which was February 20, 1945. This period was extended by a further three years and then an additional four years. In 1958 eligibility was reopened for a period expiring on September 30, 1962. From 1955 to 1958 it was available to those with unused re-establishment credit.
Up to December 31, 1961 there were 51,772 applications received for a total amount of $167,971,500. Up to that date there were 49,960 policies issued for a total face amount of $161,052,000. There were 3,045 death claims received for a total amount of $8,523,567. On December 31 there were 30,848 policies in force for a total amount of $96,876,349.
The present proposal is to extend the period of eligibility from September 30, 1962, to October 31, 1968, both for those who became eligible because of service during world war II or during the campaign in Korea.
Applications for this insurance are still coming in at an average of 125 to 130 a month.
This extension will be of particular value to those veterans who have recently assumed family responsibilities or are now becoming able to afford life insurance protection for the members of their families. subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF TIME FOR INSURANCE CONTRACTS
speechtext: Yes. The reason is exactly the same.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF TIME FOR INSURANCE CONTRACTS
speechtext: I simply wish to say this. I am very glad indeed to know that the veterans of Canada will benefit on this occasion from the minister's optimism.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF TIME FOR INSURANCE CONTRACTS
speechtext: I thought he was very pessimistic.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AUTHORITY TO BORROW

speakeroldname: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of Transport) moved
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY ACT AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AUTHORITY TO BORROW
speechtext:
that house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act to provide that the authority, with the approval of the governor in council, may from time to time borrow money from Her Majesty or otherwise to an aggregate that shall not at any time exceed $345,000,000 in lieu of $335,000,000 which it is already authorized to borrow by section 13 of the act.
